To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

upper limb amputee patients can be induced to feel touch on a rubber hand as if it were their own hand, and that this effect is accompanied by an illusion of ownership of the hand and physiological responses to threats to the artificial hand.
upper limb amputee can be induced to feel touch on a rubber hand that is placed in front of them and that they feel is their own.
upper limb amputee patients can be induced to sense touch on the artificial limb by applying synchronous tactile stimulation to the phantom limb and the artificial limb.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a prosthetic hand that can feel like a real part of the amputees body, thereby making an essential contribution to the field where the major goal is to design artificial limbs that are indistinguishable from the real thing.

the question of how the brain can be fooled into perceiving a rubber hand as one’s own, and the implications this has for the development of artificial limbs that feel as though they are part of one’s own body.
the question of how we perceive the world and how this perception can be altered by sensory feedback.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present study provides the first evidence for a successful illusion of ownership of a rubber hand in an amputee.
the illusion of ownership of a rubber hand can be extended to a phantom limb.
the illusion of ownership of the artificial limb was induced by synchronous stimulation to the stump and the artificial limb, and this was supported by quantitative and physiological data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it is possible to induce a rubber hand to be experienced as a part of one’s body, not only in sighted people, but in amputees too.
we have demonstrated that it is possible to transfer tactile sensations to a prosthetic hand by inducing a sense of body ownership.
the illusion of ownership is a powerful tool to transfer tactile sensations from the amputated limb to the artificial hand.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we show that it is possible to trick the brain into perceiving a prosthetic limb as a real part of the body.

the brain is very flexible in terms of what it considers to be part of the body, and this can be exploited for therapeutic and rehabilitation purposes, and for improving the quality of life of amputees.

it shows how the brain can be fooled into perceiving an artificial hand as its own, thereby providing a simple and effective means of transferring sensations from a stump to a prosthetically controlled hand.
